hints.title: Start with signs and domains
hints.body: Both square roots are principal, nonnegative roots. Record the restrictions on x and on the right-hand side before doing any algebra.
hints.recap: Sign and domain restrictions survive every later manipulation.
hints.pitfall: A squared equation can have solutions that fail the original equation.
hints.pause: Record the restrictions, then isolate one radical.

recall.reminder: Sign and domain restrictions survive every later manipulation.

hints.title: Square once and simplify
hints.body: Leave one square root alone on one side and square the two sides. Cancel the terms that agree, but do not immediately divide by a parameter.
hints.recap: A single squaring can reduce a two-radical equation to a simpler relation.
hints.pitfall: A parameter used as a divisor could be zero.
hints.pause: Derive the simpler relation and split any zero-divisor case from the remaining case.

recall.reminder: A single squaring can reduce a two-radical equation to a simpler relation.

hints.title: Check both necessity and existence
hints.body: In the nonzero case, use the nonnegative square root to restrict the parameter. Then construct the resulting candidate x and substitute into the original equation. Check the exceptional case separately.
hints.recap: A necessary restriction becomes sufficient only after a valid solution is exhibited.
hints.pitfall: Do not replace a principal square root of a square by a signed expression without checking its sign.
hints.pause: Combine the verified cases into the complete parameter condition.

recall.reminder: A necessary restriction becomes sufficient only after a valid solution is exhibited.

solution:
The original equation x+p+x=p requires x≥0, x+p≥0 and p≥0. If p=0, it reduces to 2x=0, solved by x=0.

For p>0, isolate x+p=p−x and square. This gives x+p=p2−2px+x, hence 2px=p2−p. Dividing by the now positive p gives 2x=p−1. Therefore p≥1 is necessary.

For every p≥1, choose x=(p−1)24. Then x+p=(p+1)24, and the two principal square roots are p−12 and p+12. Their sum is p, proving sufficiency. Together with the exceptional case, p=0 or p≥1. Answer B.
knowledgePattern: Find parameter feasibility in a radical equation without losing a zero-divisor case
